paragraphs: Predicting changes across locations and time can benefit from combining several kinds of data. However, simply adding information does not ensure that a model uses it effectively: different inputs can be poorly combined, and confounding factors can hide the relationships that matter. E²-CSTP addresses these problems alongside the computational cost of prediction.

The framework uses cross-modal attention and gates to combine information from different modalities. It then separates prediction and bias mitigation into two branches. The primary branch makes the spatio-temporal forecast, while an auxiliary branch models additional modalities and applies causal interventions. This arrangement is intended to help distinguish causal dependencies from misleading associations in the combined data.

For efficiency, the model combines graph convolutional networks with Mamba to encode spatial and temporal information. Across four real-world datasets, the authors report better results than nine comparison methods, with accuracy improvements reaching 9.66% and computational overhead reductions ranging from 17.37% to 56.11%. These findings support the framework’s joint emphasis on information fusion, causal modeling, and efficient computation.
neurips-2025-causal-spatio-temporal-pred.tldr: E²-CSTP combines multimodal fusion, causal interventions, and efficient spatial-temporal encoding to improve prediction accuracy while reducing computation.

paragraphs: An image enlargement model can produce convincing results at its training scale yet struggle when asked for much greater magnification. Chain-of-Zoom addresses this by breaking an extreme enlargement into a sequence of intermediate zoom levels. Each step reuses an existing super-resolution model, making the large transformation a chain of smaller conditional generation problems.

As magnification increases, the remaining visual evidence becomes less informative. The framework therefore supplies each step with text guidance produced by a vision-language model and tailored to multiple scales. Its prompt extractor is fine-tuned using Generalized Reward Policy Optimization and a critic vision-language model, with the aim of making the guidance better match human preferences.

The distinction between these components matters: the super-resolution backbone can be reused without additional training, while the prompt extractor receives preference-oriented training. Experiments show that a standard diffusion model designed for 4× super-resolution can, within this framework, produce enlargements beyond 256× with high reported perceptual quality and fidelity. The contribution is a reusable procedure for extending a model’s effective zoom range.
neurips-2025-chain-of-zoom-extreme-super.tldr: Chain-of-Zoom repeatedly applies a super-resolution model with scale-aware text guidance to achieve enlargements beyond 256×.

paragraphs: Generating a molecule that binds strongly to a target protein addresses only part of the drug-design problem. The molecule also needs to be feasible to synthesize and selective about its targets. This paper argues that evaluations centered mainly on binding affinity overlook these other properties, making it harder to judge practical usefulness.

The authors identify limitations in guiding conventional diffusion generators toward this broader set of objectives. Their proposed framework, CByG, extends Bayesian Flow Networks into a conditional generator that incorporates gradients associated with desired molecular properties. This gives property-specific guidance a direct role in shaping the generation of three-dimensional molecules.

The work also introduces an evaluation scheme covering binding affinity, synthetic feasibility, and selectivity together. In extensive experiments, CByG significantly outperforms the compared models across multiple essential criteria. The stated contribution therefore concerns both generation and assessment: it offers a more controllable molecular generator and tests it against a broader definition of success relevant to practical drug discovery.
neurips-2025-controllable-3d-molecular-g.tldr: CByG guides 3D molecular generation toward binding affinity, synthetic feasibility, and selectivity using a gradient-conditioned Bayesian Flow Network.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to choose a nonempty set whose value per element is as small or large as possible. The underlying set function is submodular or supermodular, structures that describe how the value of adding an element changes with the surrounding set. The formulation connects problems such as finding dense subgraphs and minimizing submodular functions.

The authors broaden ratio problems to allow negative values and functions that are not monotone. Using classical results, they establish strongly polynomial-time reductions between several seemingly different optimization problems. A shared geometric formulation, based on a minimum norm point in a base polyhedron, explains how algorithms can transfer between them. This makes SuperGreedy++ and Wolfe’s minimum norm point algorithm applicable throughout the connected problem family.

More than 400 experiments cover seven problem types and datasets reaching approximately 100 million edges. On concrete problems such as HNSN, general optimization methods outperform specialized baselines by orders of magnitude. These results challenge assumptions about which algorithm families scale effectively and show the practical value of recognizing equivalence between differently formulated tasks.
neurips-2025-corporate-needs-you-to-find.tldr: Several submodular and supermodular optimization problems share an equivalent structure, allowing general algorithms to outperform specialized methods on concrete tasks.

paragraphs: Event cameras record changes in pixel intensity asynchronously, offering useful temporal resolution and dynamic range for estimating depth under difficult lighting. Training depth models from these signals is harder when the available LiDAR supervision is sparse, incomplete, or affected by artifacts. Distil-E2D strengthens that supervision by transferring knowledge from image-based depth models.

The framework uses foundation depth models to generate dense pseudolabels from conventional APS or RGB frames recorded alongside the events. These predictions complement the sparse LiDAR measurements. Because synthetic and measured depths can disagree, a confidence-guided loss learns a nonlinear alignment between them and adjusts the contribution of supervision according to confidence in that alignment.

Two architectural choices further support learning. A Context Transformer incorporates earlier predictions, and a dual-decoder training scheme teaches the encoder both metric depth and relative depth relationships. Benchmark experiments report state-of-the-art performance for both event-only and event-plus-APS settings. The findings show how dense image-derived knowledge, calibrated against measured depth, can improve learning from sparse event signals.
neurips-2025-distil-e2d-distilling-image.tldr: Distil-E2D improves event-camera depth estimation by combining image-derived dense pseudolabels, sparse LiDAR supervision, and confidence-aware depth calibration.

paragraphs: Fully connected feedforward layers can consume substantial computation and memory inside neural networks. EUGens introduces a broader class of dense layers intended to reduce these costs while retaining the expressive power and adaptability associated with conventional layers. The design also brings existing efficient feedforward extensions into a common formulation.

EUGens uses random features to approximate standard feedforward computations and adds a direct dependence on input norms. The authors report a reduction in inference complexity from quadratic to linear time. They also present what they identify as the first unbiased approximation algorithms for feedforward layers with arbitrary polynomial activations. Unbiasedness concerns the approximation’s average behavior, rather than requiring every individual approximation to be exact.

A separate layer-wise knowledge-transfer method adapts EUGens to pretrained networks without backpropagation. Experiments incorporate the layers into Transformers and multilayer perceptrons for image classification, language-model pretraining, and 3D scene reconstruction. Reported improvements reach 27% in inference speed and 30% in memory efficiency, supporting their potential for deployment where computational resources are constrained.
neurips-2025-eugens-efficient-unified-an.tldr: EUGens uses random-feature dense layers and layer-wise knowledge transfer to reduce neural-network inference costs while preserving expressive capability.

paragraphs: A model’s ability to answer a problem immediately does not fully describe how well it can benefit from experience. EvaLearn evaluates this second capability by presenting problems sequentially, allowing earlier solutions to inform later ones. Its 648 challenging problems cover six task types and are organized into 182 sequences, each focused on one type.

The benchmark provides five automated metrics for assessing learning capability and efficiency. Tests of nine frontier models reveal different patterns: some begin with moderate performance and improve strongly, while others gain little from previous experience or exhibit negative transfer. Claude-3.7-sonnet is highlighted as an example of the former pattern.

The authors also examine two learning settings and find that instance-level rubrics and feedback from a teacher model can help learning. Across tasks, stronger static performance does not consistently translate into stronger learning capability. The benchmark therefore adds a distinct evaluation perspective: assessing how a model’s performance develops through a sequence, alongside what it can already do when problems are assessed independently.
neurips-2025-evalearn-quantifying-the-le.tldr: EvaLearn measures how LLMs improve through sequential problem solving and finds that strong initial performance does not consistently predict stronger learning.

paragraphs: Time-series classification often has access to many recordings but relatively few labels. Virtual Adversarial Training helps use unlabeled examples by encouraging predictions to remain stable under challenging perturbations. Straightforward applications can nevertheless perform poorly when those perturbations ignore the temporal organization of the signal.

Functional Virtual Adversarial Training, or f-VAT, incorporates that organization into how perturbations are constructed. The authors establish a theoretical duality between the norm used to measure a perturbation and the model’s sensitivity to changes in the underlying function. They use this relationship to motivate a Sobolev H⁻ˢ norm for generating structured adversarial changes to time-series data.

The choice of norm matters because it determines which disturbances the training procedure asks the classifier to withstand. By reflecting functional structure, f-VAT makes that pressure more appropriate for time-dependent observations. Extensive semi-supervised classification experiments report better performance than recent methods, with improvements reaching approximately 9%. Additional visualizations provide further insight into the method’s behavior and its reported advantages.
neurips-2025-functional-virtual-adversar.tldr: f-VAT improves semi-supervised time-series classification by constructing adversarial perturbations that account for the signal’s functional structure.

paragraphs: Speculative decoding speeds up language-model inference by producing multiple candidate tokens through a draft process. Its effectiveness can suffer when token relationships during draft-model training do not align with those encountered during decoding. GRIFFIN targets this mismatch through coordinated changes to the training procedure and the draft model itself.

During training, a loss mask excludes highly misaligned tokens from the optimization objective. This prevents those tokens from steering the draft model in unhelpful directions. The draft architecture also introduces input tokens to correct inconsistencies in generated features. Together, these mechanisms address both the training signal and the representations used to propose tokens.

Experiments cover LLaMA, Vicuna, Qwen, and Mixtral models. The authors report an average acceptance-length improvement above 8% and an improvement in speedup ratio exceeding 7% relative to current leading speculative-decoding methods. The results connect better token alignment with longer accepted drafts and faster inference, showing that how a draft model is trained and conditioned can materially affect acceleration.
neurips-2025-griffin-effective-token-ali.tldr: GRIFFIN improves speculative decoding by aligning draft-model training and token features with decoding behavior, increasing accepted draft length and speed.

paragraphs: Training a parameterized quantum circuit requires estimating how its objective changes with each parameter. This is difficult because quantum states occupy exponentially large mathematical spaces and measurements reveal only limited information. The paper develops a gradient-estimation framework that uses the circuit’s Lie algebraic structure together with the Hadamard test.

By analyzing derivatives of matrix exponentials within Lie algebras, the authors express the gradient as a weighted combination of expectation values accessible through Hadamard tests. The weights depend only on the circuit’s parameterization and can be computed efficiently. Shadow tomography techniques can then be used to estimate the required expectation values.

Within this framework, the required measurement shots scale logarithmically with the number of parameters, while classical and quantum computation take polynomial time. The authors describe this as an exponential reduction in measurement cost and a polynomial time improvement over existing work. The result establishes the sufficiency of this structured approach for efficient gradient estimation; its mechanism specifically depends on exploiting the circuit’s algebraic organization.
neurips-2025-hadamard-test-is-sufficient.tldr: Exploiting Lie algebraic circuit structure allows Hadamard-test-based quantum gradient estimation with logarithmic measurement-shot scaling in the parameter count.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a moving 3D scene from a single-camera video requires a representation that changes coherently over time. Extending Gaussian Splatting to this setting can involve unnecessary updates in static regions, weak motion supervision, and difficulty representing complex deformations. HAIF-GS addresses these issues through a sparse set of anchors that drive deformation.

An Anchor Filter first identifies regions where motion matters, suppressing redundant updates elsewhere. A self-supervised deformation module then combines features from multiple frames to induce anchor motion without explicit flow labels. For more detailed movement, hierarchical anchor propagation increases anchor resolution according to motion complexity and passes transformations across levels.

These components connect where the model allocates motion updates, how it learns movement, and how finely it represents deformation. Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks report significant improvements over prior dynamic Gaussian Splatting methods in rendering quality, consistency across time, and reconstruction efficiency. The findings support structured anchor-based motion as a way to improve both reconstruction coherence and computational use.
neurips-2025-haif-gs-hierarchical-and-in.tldr: HAIF-GS uses filtered, hierarchically refined motion anchors to improve dynamic Gaussian Splatting reconstruction without explicit flow labels.

paragraphs: Discrete diffusion models can learn a data distribution well yet still generate poor samples when sampling is accelerated. Reducing the number of steps can allow approximation errors to accumulate, creating a gap between model quality and the quality of its outputs. This paper addresses that gap through the sampling procedure.

The proposed predictor-corrector scheme uses information from the diffusion model to guide its corrective updates. These updates are intended to counter accumulating errors more reliably. The authors also introduce complementary changes based on hollow transformers and a tailored training objective that makes use of more training signal. A synthetic example illustrates existing samplers’ failure modes and how the informed corrector alleviates them.

On Text8, the approach generates text with significantly fewer errors than the comparison methods. On tokenized ImageNet at 256×256 resolution, it produces better samples with fewer steps, as reflected in improved FID scores. Together, these results show that better-informed corrections can improve the trade-off between sampling cost and output quality in discrete diffusion.
neurips-2025-informed-correctors-for-dis.tldr: Model-informed corrective updates reduce sampling errors in discrete diffusion, improving text and image generation with fewer steps.

paragraphs: A visual question-answering model can learn to guess from question wording instead of inspecting the image. Correlations between question templates and answers make this shortcut tempting, especially damaging performance when evaluation data differ from training data. This paper investigates how the imbalance develops and proposes a method to reduce it.

The authors’ empirical and theoretical analysis links language bias to unequal gradients across modalities. Differences inherent in multimodal data produce this imbalance, which then distorts feature fusion and classifier weights. Their Multi-Margin Collaborative Debiasing framework responds with adaptive angular margins that account for answer frequency, confidence, and difficulty.

The framework also uses contrastive learning whose behavior changes with difficulty, working alongside the margins to reshape decision boundaries. This connects the proposed explanation of bias with interventions in both representation learning and classification. Across multiple challenging VQA benchmarks, the authors report consistently better resistance to language bias than leading comparison methods. The contribution combines an account of the training dynamics behind the shortcut with a coordinated method for addressing it.
neurips-2025-languagebiasresilient-visua.tldr: MMCD addresses language shortcuts in visual question answering through adaptive classification margins and difficulty-aware contrastive learning.

paragraphs: Different layers of the same pretrained language model can be better suited to different downstream tasks. Methods that rank layers using only weight statistics or other model-centered heuristics can miss the role of training data. LayerIF estimates layer quality using both the model’s gradients and the influence of examples on validation performance.

The framework isolates gradients associated with each layer and uses influence functions to estimate how training examples affect validation loss through that layer. These measurements produce data-driven importance scores. Because the scores depend on the evaluation task, a single model can receive different layer rankings for different applications, revealing task-specific specialization.

The authors use these scores for two allocation problems: distributing experts in LoRA-MoE architectures and assigning different sparsity levels to layers during pruning. Experiments across multiple language-model architectures show consistent task-performance gains from influence-guided allocation. This demonstrates a practical use for the estimates: they can guide where to place adaptation resources and how to distribute pruning within a model.
neurips-2025-layerif-estimating-layer-qu.tldr: LayerIF uses layer-wise influence functions to estimate task-specific importance and improve expert allocation and pruning in language models.

paragraphs: Speculative decoding accelerates language-model inference without sacrificing accuracy, but it has often been considered mainly useful for dense models. This paper shows that mixture-of-experts models can benefit more at medium batch sizes. It further predicts that increasing model sparsity broadens the batch-size range in which speculative decoding is expected to help.

The authors develop a theoretical model of the relevant trade-offs. A key observation is that a high draft-token acceptance rate does not by itself ensure strong acceleration: workload and architecture changes can still reduce the benefit. They introduce target efficiency as an additional metric to capture these effects and help identify system bottlenecks.

Experiments on different GPUs validate the theoretical predictions and report speedups reaching 2.29× for Qwen2-57B-A14B at medium batch sizes. The result is particularly relevant to serving scenarios, including private deployments, where existing acceleration approaches struggle. Its broader message is that speculative-decoding performance depends jointly on acceptance behavior, model sparsity, workload, and the efficiency of target-model execution.
neurips-2025-moesd-unveil-speculative-de.tldr: Sparse mixture-of-experts models can benefit strongly from speculative decoding at medium batch sizes, with reported speedups up to 2.29×.

paragraphs: In a two-person conversation, listener responses include both speech and facial behavior, and their timing needs to fit together. This paper introduces an online task that generates these responses from a speaker’s multimodal inputs. The challenge includes producing appropriate content while keeping the generated audio synchronized with the listener’s face.

OmniResponse uses text as an intermediate connection between speech and facial responses. Built around a pretrained language model, it generates multimodal responses autoregressively. Chrono-Text Markup attaches precise timestamps to generated text tokens, while TempoVoice provides controllable online text-to-speech generation. Together, these components coordinate spoken output with facial behavior.

The authors also introduce ResponseNet, containing 696 detailed two-person interactions with synchronized split-screen video, multichannel audio, transcripts, and annotated facial behaviors. Evaluations on this dataset show improvements over baseline models in speech meaning, audiovisual synchronization, and generation quality. The work contributes both a generation system and a dataset for studying listener behavior as a coordinated, ongoing multimodal response.
neurips-2025-omniresponse-online-multimo.tldr: OmniResponse coordinates online speech and facial listener responses using timestamped text and controllable speech generation.

paragraphs: Research on AI alignment needs a shared understanding of what alignment means. This position paper argues that unclear or inconsistent definitions impede progress and collaboration across disciplines. It examines alignment as a changing relationship between people and AI systems, with adaptation occurring on both sides of that relationship.

The authors systematically review more than 400 papers across human-computer interaction, natural-language processing, machine learning, and other fields. Building on how those papers define and implement alignment, they propose the Bidirectional Human-AI Alignment framework. It includes established efforts to fit AI systems to human values alongside support for people’s cognitive, behavioral, and societal adaptation to advancing AI.

The review identifies gaps in long-term interaction design, modeling human values, and mutual understanding. The paper concludes with three central challenges and actionable research recommendations. Its contribution is a conceptual and research-organizing framework: it asks researchers to make their definitions explicit and account for how sustained interaction changes both human expectations and AI-related practices.
neurips-2025-position-towards-bidirectio.tldr: This position paper frames alignment as a dynamic, bidirectional relationship that includes adapting AI to people and supporting people’s adaptation to AI.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that rapidly generated, individually tailored media could create a new form of compulsive digital consumption. Its concern centers on systems that adjust content within seconds while pursuing engagement-maximizing incentives. The phrase “digital heroin” expresses the authors’ warning about potentially severe dependence-like effects.

The argument draws on interdisciplinary work, including clinical observations of social-media addiction and research on dopamine-related feedback. The authors connect these findings to the possibility that real-time content tailoring could weaken user autonomy and contribute to emotional distress. They emphasize adolescents and other vulnerable groups, alongside potential consequences for cognitive development and social stability.

The paper calls for strong government oversight comparable to controls on addictive substances, particularly where minors are concerned. It also urges machine-learning researchers to establish design guidelines, work with public-health specialists, and support targeted policies. These are preventive recommendations grounded in the authors’ assessment of a developing risk, rather than a report that all personalized generative systems have already produced the predicted harms.
neurips-2025-real-time-hyper-personalize.tldr: This position paper calls for oversight and preventive design measures against addiction-like risks from real-time, engagement-driven personalized generative media.

paragraphs: This paper studies kernel ridge regression when observation noise has heavy tails, while still possessing a finite number of higher moments. The question is whether regularized least squares can retain strong statistical performance under weaker noise assumptions than those commonly used to establish its convergence rates.

The authors derive excess-risk bounds using an integral-operator framework. The bounds contain both a subgaussian component and a polynomial component. The dominant subgaussian part permits convergence rates previously established under subexponential noise assumptions. Their proof relies on a Fuk–Nagaev inequality for random variables taking values in a Hilbert space, connecting concentration behavior to the regression analysis.

Under standard conditions on eigenvalue decay, the resulting rates are minimax optimal. This establishes asymptotic robustness of regularized least squares in the heavy-tailed setting covered by the analysis. The conditions are central to the result: the claim concerns noise with the stated finite moments and optimal rates under the specified spectral assumptions, rather than unrestricted noise distributions.
neurips-2025-regularized-least-squares-l.tldr: Kernel ridge regression achieves minimax-optimal convergence rates under heavy-tailed noise with suitable finite moments and standard eigenvalue-decay conditions.

paragraphs: World models predict how a state will change after an action. Training them to maximize the likelihood of observed sequences does not always align with the properties users care about, such as transition accuracy or visual quality. RLVR-World addresses this mismatch by directly optimizing task-relevant measures through reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards.

The framework represents world modeling as autoregressive prediction over tokenized sequences. Crucially, it evaluates the decoded predictions to obtain rewards, so the learning signal reflects the resulting language or video output. This connects optimization to measurable properties of the predicted transition rather than relying exclusively on the likelihood of its token sequence.

The authors demonstrate substantial gains for both language-based and video-based world models across text games, web navigation, and robot manipulation. These findings indicate that verifiable-reward reinforcement learning may be useful beyond reasoning language models. The proposed broader implication is a promising post-training approach for making generative models better serve the particular tasks their outputs are meant to support.
neurips-2025-rlvr-world-training-world-m.tldr: RLVR-World improves world models by using measurable properties of decoded predictions as reinforcement-learning rewards.

paragraphs: Synthetic histopathology images need to preserve both mixtures of tissue types and subtle morphological details. This paper conditions a latent diffusion model on two complementary inputs: segmentation maps specify tissue regions, while raw tissue crops provide visual information from the corresponding regions. The combination supports controlled generation with region-wise annotations.

For annotated datasets, the authors extract patches with 20–80% tissue heterogeneity. For unannotated whole-slide images, they use foundation-model embeddings to cluster tissue into 100 types and generate pseudo-semantic training maps. This self-supervised extension allows the method to use 11,765 TCGA slides without manual annotations.

The reported image-distribution Fréchet Distance falls from 430.1 to 72.0 on Camelyon16, with two- to threefold reductions on Panda and TCGA. DeepLabv3+ segmentation models trained only on synthetic images achieve test IoU scores of 0.71 and 0.95 on Camelyon16 and Panda, compared with real-data results of 0.72 and 0.96. These findings demonstrate practical downstream value alongside improved synthesis quality.
neurips-2025-semantic-and-visual-crop-gu.tldr: Combining tissue-region maps with raw visual crops produces controlled histopathology images that support segmentation performance close to real-data training.

paragraphs: Colorizing an anime facial sketch from a reference image requires preserving the sketch’s structure while adopting stylistic attributes from the reference. SSIMBaD tackles this through a continuous-time diffusion framework. Its focus is on how the noise process changes perceived image structure throughout generation.

Predefined noise schedules can create uneven perceptual changes along the diffusion trajectory. SSIMBaD transforms sigma space so that degradation measured by structural similarity follows a linear progression. This scaling aims to distribute visual difficulty uniformly across timesteps, making the reconstruction process more balanced and helping it stay faithful to the input sketch.

The central idea is to organize diffusion around a perceptual measure rather than assume that a conventional noise schedule already produces consistent visual changes. On a large anime-face dataset, the authors report state-of-the-art preservation of structure together with strong perceptual quality. They also report robust generalization across different styles and structural variations, supporting the value of perceptually guided scaling for this colorization task.
neurips-2025-ssimbad-sigma-scaling-with-.tldr: SSIMBaD uses structural-similarity-guided diffusion scaling to color anime face sketches while preserving their structure and transferring reference style.

paragraphs: A ReLU network divides its input space into regions within which its behavior is linear. Counting those regions is an established way to describe expressive power, but researchers use several definitions that are not equivalent. This paper first maps those definitions across the literature and explains how they relate.

It then analyzes the computational difficulty of counting regions under the different definitions. The authors prove NP-hardness and #P-hardness results even for networks with a single hidden layer. For networks with two or more hidden layers, they also establish strong hardness results for approximation, showing that relaxing exact counting does not generally remove the difficulty.

On the positive side, counting is possible using polynomial space for some common definitions. That is a memory bound and does not establish a polynomial-time algorithm. Together, the results clarify both what is being counted and the computational resources involved. They show why a mathematically useful measure of network expressiveness can nevertheless be difficult to calculate for a given network.
neurips-2025-the-computational-complexit.tldr: Counting ReLU linear regions is generally computationally hard, even in shallow networks, although some definitions permit polynomial-space algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper develops a mathematical foundation for causal inference using a topos, a categorical setting with its own internal logic. It introduces topos causal models as a strict generalization of structural causal models. The aim is to describe causal mechanisms, interventions, and counterfactual reasoning within one coherent mathematical framework.

Sheaf theory supplies a way to combine local causal mechanisms into a consistent global function. A structure called a subobject classifier provides a general mechanism for defining interventions. The authors show that this classifier is generally governed by a Heyting algebra rather than Boolean logic, leading to an intuitionistic internal language for causal reasoning. They specify that language and its associated semantics.

The main theorem establishes a universal property: any causal functor mapping decomposable structure to probabilistic semantics factors uniquely through a topos causal-model representation. In plain terms, mappings satisfying that description pass through the proposed framework in a uniquely determined way. This is a structural result about organizing causal representations and reasoning, rather than an empirical prediction-performance claim.
neurips-2025-universal-causal-inference-.tldr: Topos causal models generalize structural causal models and provide a unified mathematical treatment of causal mechanisms, interventions, and internal reasoning.

paragraphs: Two-stage image generation first compresses images into latent tokens and then learns to generate those tokens. Better reconstruction at the compression stage need not produce better generation overall. This paper studies the trade-off in discrete autoregressive generation and shows that smaller generators can benefit from stronger compression even when reconstruction becomes worse.

The authors analyze how generation compute interacts with the tokenizer’s rate-distortion trade-off. They introduce Causally Regularized Tokenization, which uses knowledge of the later generation procedure to shape the latent representation. It makes tokens easier to model without changing the compression rate and with only a marginal effect on distortion, yielding reported compute-efficiency improvements of two to three times.

With further tokenizer optimizations, the pipeline matches LlamaGen-3B’s reported generation performance of 2.18 FID using 256 rather than 576 tokens per image and 775 million rather than 3.1 billion total parameters. Architecture and inference procedure remain the same. The result supports designing tokenizers around the capacity and needs of the downstream generator.
neurips-2025-when-worse-is-better-naviga.tldr: Visual tokenizers can improve generation by making compressed tokens easier to model, even when reconstruction quality is slightly worse.
